The step you should do next is measuring specific evaluation metrics that are chosen according to the type of problem you are trying to solve, and based on that, you can reach a conclusion of how well your model performs. And even problems within a specific type, such as **classification** and **regression**, which both fall under *supervised learning*, have their own separate set of evaluation metrics that they use. These are only a subset of the evaluation metrics that are used with these two types of supervised learning problems. The focus of this article will be on *classification evaluation metrics*, specifically the following four: **Accuracy, Precision, Recall,** and **F1 Score.**. When getting started with machine learning, the first examples that people tend to go through are simple classification problems, such as the cat vs dog classification problem I’ve previously mentioned in this article. The evaluation metric used to measure how good the model for that problem performs is *accuracy*, which can simply be defined as the following:. To very simply showcase its implementation, consider that you are working with a *binary classification* problem, which means that you are working with *True Positives (TP), True Negatives (TN), False Positives (FP),* and *False Negatives (FN).*. To work with such data, we usually use other metrics, such as *precision* and *recall*. > **out of all of the actual positive classes in my dataset, how many of them was my model able to ‘remember’, or ‘recall’?**. If you are able to remember all 8 positive instances, then you have a *recall of 100%!* However, if you can only remember 5 of those 8 days that you have had iced coffee during, and you answer with 5, then you would have a *recall of 62.5%.* Why is that?
